titleZh: 代数、函数与三角学：建立运动几何的基础
titleEn: Algebra, functions, and trigonometry: the foundation of motion geometry
title: Algebra, functions, and trigonometry: the foundation of motion geometry

blocks.text: Manipulator poses, camera fields of view, blade inclinations, and trajectory periodicity all rely on algebra and trigonometry. The goal is not to memorize formulas again, but to see which geometric relation a formula describes and verify it with code.
4.1 An equation is another form of a constraint

Assembly problems often ask which condition a quantity must satisfy. A 2-D point $p=(x,y)$ on a circle of radius $r$ satisfies $x^2+y^2=r^2$. This is not an isolated algebra exercise; it is a minimal model for reachable boundaries, trajectory constraints, and collision geometry.
Writing the constraint as $g=0$ lets us check the residual $|g|$ in code. In more complex robot models, the residual becomes a metric for optimization and experiment evaluation.

blocks.code:
import numpy as np

radius_m = 0.25
point_m = np.array([0.15, 0.20])
residual = point_m @ point_m - radius_m**2
print(f"constraint residual = {residual:.3e}")

blocks.text: 4.2 A function graph visualizes a model

A function graph makes the relation between input and output observable. Sine and cosine are not only exam formulas; they describe rotations, periodic motion, and joint trajectories. Plot first, then discuss amplitude, phase, and period, so symbols do not become decoration.

blocks.code:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

t = np.linspace(0.0, 4.0, 400)
q0, amplitude, omega, phase = 0.2, 0.5, 2.0, 0.3
q = q0 + amplitude * np.sin(omega * t + phase)

plt.plot(t, q)
plt.xlabel("time [s]")
plt.ylabel("joint angle [rad]")
plt.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
plt.show()

blocks.text: Changing $A$ changes the motion range, changing $\omega$ changes the speed, and changing $\phi$ changes the initial state. Every change should be explained in physical language, not merely described as “the curve changed.”
4.3 Angles, radians, and the unit circle

Trigonometric functions usually take radians because the ratio of arc length to radius keeps derivative formulas simple: $\frac{d}{d\theta}\sin\theta=\cos\theta$. Code libraries almost always expect radians. Mixing degrees and radians is one of the most common and subtle foundational errors in robot programs.

blocks.code:
import numpy as np

angle_deg = 30.0
angle_rad = np.deg2rad(angle_deg)
assert np.isclose(np.rad2deg(angle_rad), angle_deg)
print(np.sin(angle_rad))

blocks.title: Failure diagnosis: a plausible curve can still be wrong

blocks.text: Passing 30 directly to `np.sin` does not raise an error because 30 is a valid number. It is interpreted as 30 radians rather than 30 degrees. Convert units at the interface and preserve unit semantics in names or data structures.
4.4 Inverse trigonometric functions and pose estimation

When a sensor gives a direction vector $(v_x,v_y)$, use `atan2(v_y,v_x)` to obtain its heading. `atan2` handles quadrants, unlike $\arctan(v_y/v_x)$, which loses sign information and fails when $v_x=0$.

blocks.code:
import numpy as np

direction = np.array([-1.0, 1.0])
heading_rad = np.arctan2(direction[1], direction[0])
heading_deg = np.rad2deg(heading_rad)
print(f"heading = {heading_deg:.1f} deg")

blocks.text: 4.5 Absolute values, inequalities, and safety boundaries

“Error must be below 0.2 mm” is the absolute-value inequality $|e|\le0.2$; a force limit is $F_{\min}\le F\le F_{\max}$. Absolute value folds direction into magnitude, useful for safety and anomaly detection, but signed error must also be kept when direction has physical meaning.

blocks.code:
def within_interval(value, lower, upper, tolerance=0.0):
    value = np.asarray(value, dtype=float)
    lower, upper = float(lower), float(upper)
    if lower > upper or tolerance < 0:
        raise ValueError("invalid interval")
    return bool(np.all(value >= lower - tolerance) and
                np.all(value <= upper + tolerance))

assert within_interval([0.0, 0.1], -0.2, 0.2)
assert not within_interval([0.25], -0.2, 0.2)

blocks.text: 4.6 Exponentials, logarithms, and scale changes

Exponentials and logarithms appear in probability, losses, sensor dynamic range, and time constants. $e^x$ maps additive scale to multiplicative scale; $\log$ maps products to sums. In optimization, log-likelihood is more stable than multiplying probabilities. Contact force, image brightness, and rewards can span orders of magnitude, so ask about scale before choosing a function.

Computing $\exp(1000)$ directly overflows and breaks later gradients and normalization. Use log-sum-exp, softplus, or subtract the maximum first. Numerical stability is part of the model definition, not an afterthought.
4.7 Trigonometric identities and coordinate projection

The identity $\sin(\alpha+\beta)=\sin\alpha\cos\beta+\cos\alpha\sin\beta$ explains why serial-joint angles add: the second link direction rotates by $\beta$ relative to the first. Projection formulas $v_x=\|v\|\cos\theta,\ v_y=\|v\|\sin\theta$ convert polar to Cartesian coordinates. Draw the vector before writing the identity.
4.8 Phase, frequency, and sampling of periodic functions

The period of $q(t)=A\sin(\omega t+\phi)$ is $T=2\pi/\omega$. Sampling too slowly creates aliasing: a fast motion may appear slow and become impossible to identify. Configure sampling from the highest frequency of interest and log both raw rate and resampling method.

blocks.code:
def sinusoid_trajectory(t, offset, amplitude, omega, phase):
    t = np.asarray(t, dtype=float)
    value = offset + amplitude * np.sin(omega * t + phase)
    velocity = amplitude * omega * np.cos(omega * t + phase)
    acceleration = -amplitude * omega**2 * np.sin(omega * t + phase)
    return value, velocity, acceleration

t = np.linspace(0., 2. * np.pi, 101)
q, qdot, qddot = sinusoid_trajectory(t, 0., 1., 1., 0.)
assert np.isclose(q[0], q[-1], atol=1e-12)

blocks.text: 4.9 Scaling analysis: does the equation make physical sense

Dimensional analysis is the cheapest error check. Position error cannot be added directly to angle error; combine them only through a radius, a Jacobian, or an explicit weight. Torque is N m, power is N m/s, and probability is dimensionless. Put units in variable names and plot axes to bridge formulas and code.
If position and orientation tolerances are $e_p^\mathrm{max}$ and $e_\theta^\mathrm{max}$, use
This is not the only choice, but every term is dimensionless and interpretable. Changing tolerances changes the task and must be reported.

blocks.title: Three hand checks before the complete lab

blocks.text: Take $e_p=1\,\mathrm{mm}$, $e_p^{\max}=2\,\mathrm{mm}$, $e_\theta=0.01\,\mathrm{rad}$, and $e_\theta^{\max}=0.02\,\mathrm{rad}$ and hand-calculate $J=0.5$. Express one direction as both $(r,\theta)$ and $(x,y)$ and check the quadrant. Finally set $A=0.4$ and $\omega=2.3$ and explain why velocity amplitude is $0.92$ and acceleration amplitude is $2.116$. The three checks freeze normalization, coordinate representation, and derivative scale.
4.10 Complete algebra and trigonometry lab: from symbols to robot trajectories

This lab does not append unrelated NumPy functions. It connects five mathematical threads into one causal chain: intervals represent constraints, stable functions handle extreme scales, polar coordinates represent planar direction, sinusoids generate continuous trajectories, and dimensionless error combines task metrics with different units. Every function declares its domain before computing; invalid domains fail at the mathematical boundary rather than becoming NaN, a wrong quadrant, or an unsafe action inside the controller.

blocks.title: Why analytic and numerical derivatives must check each other

blocks.text: For a sinusoid, $\dot q=A\omega\cos(\omega t+\phi)$ and $\ddot q=-A\omega^2\sin(\omega t+\phi)$. The analytic form shows that amplitudes scale with $\omega$ and $\omega^2$; a central finite difference independently checks sign and scale from sampled data. When they disagree, inspect time units, radians, sampling interval, and boundary points before tuning controller gains. The test compares interior samples because one-sided endpoint differences have a different truncation error.

blocks.caption: 代数、三角、轨迹和无量纲误差完整主源 / Complete algebra, trigonometry, trajectory, and dimensionless-error source

blocks.text: The tests require more than returning a number. Polar round trips freeze quadrant semantics; analytic-versus-finite-difference velocity freezes derivative semantics; softplus at $x=\pm1000$ freezes numerical stability; and zero direction, NaN, and zero tolerance deliberately construct counterexamples. A round-trip failure localizes to angle and quadrant, a derivative failure to time and scale, an extreme-value failure to the numerical formula, and an unreported invalid input to interface admission.

blocks.caption: 代数与三角完整契约测试 / Complete algebra-and-trigonometry contract tests
blocks.code:
import unittest

import numpy as np

from algebra_trig_lab import (
    AlgebraTrigContractError,
    cartesian_to_polar,
    dimensionless_error,
    polar_to_cartesian,
    sinusoid_trajectory,
    softplus_stable,
    within_interval,
)


class AlgebraTrigTests(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_interval_and_stable_softplus(self):
        self.assertTrue(within_interval([0., .1], -.2, .2))
        self.assertFalse(within_interval([.3], -.2, .2))
        self.assertTrue(np.all(np.isfinite(softplus_stable([1000., -1000.]))))

    def test_polar_round_trip(self):
        point = polar_to_cartesian(2.0, .7)
        radius, angle = cartesian_to_polar(point)
        self.assertAlmostEqual(radius, 2.0)
        self.assertAlmostEqual(angle, .7)

    def test_sinusoid_derivatives_and_dimensionless_error(self):
        t = np.linspace(0., 2. * np.pi, 101)
        q, qdot, qddot = sinusoid_trajectory(t, 0., 1., 1., 0.)
        self.assertAlmostEqual(q[0], q[-1])
        self.assertAlmostEqual(qdot[0], 1.0)
        self.assertAlmostEqual(qddot[0], 0.0)
        self.assertAlmostEqual(dimensionless_error(.001, .01, .002, .02), .5)

    def test_analytic_velocity_matches_finite_difference(self):
        t = np.linspace(0.1, 1.0, 1001)
        q, qdot, _ = sinusoid_trajectory(t, .2, .4, 2.3, -.1)
        numerical = np.gradient(q, t)
        self.assertLess(np.max(np.abs(numerical[1:-1] - qdot[1:-1])), 2e-6)

    def test_invalid_contracts_fail_at_the_boundary(self):
        with self.assertRaises(AlgebraTrigContractError):
            within_interval([np.nan], 0., 1.)
        with self.assertRaises(AlgebraTrigContractError):
            cartesian_to_polar([0., 0.])
        with self.assertRaises(AlgebraTrigContractError):
            dimensionless_error(.1, .1, 0., 1.)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    unittest.main()

blocks.text: At this point, observe where these basic quantities will enter later components: joint outputs enter forward kinematics, angular rates enter the Jacobian, dimensionless error enters optimization, and interval checks enter the safety layer of a policy. Vectors, matrices, and Jacobians are defined later; this paragraph only marks the route and does not require computing them now.
4.11 Chapter recap and research exit

This chapter treated equations as constraints, functions as input-output models, and trigonometric functions as the language of rotation and periodic motion. Finish by plotting $\sin\theta$ and $\cos\theta$, comparing `atan` with `atan2`, and connecting periodic joint trajectories to 2R forward kinematics. Explain how parameters determine range, speed, and period.

Minimum check: convert an angle between degrees and radians and verify the round-trip error; compare `atan` and `atan2` on the same direction vector; then describe in words how a periodic joint trajectory will enter 2R forward kinematics, without computing matrices now.
